title: Determinants of age at menarche in the UK: analyses from the Breakthrough Generations Study.
ehr_evidence: Age at menarche data were collected retrospectively by questionnaire from 81 606 women aged 16 – 98, resident in the UK and participating in the Breakthrough Generations Study.
summary: A cohort study of 81,606 UK women (aged 16–98) using baseline questionnaire data to identify pre- and post-natal determinants of age at menarche.
key_findings: Birthweight was positively associated with age at menarche (per 500 g increase: multivariate beta = 1.24 months, 95% CI 1.10–1.37, Ptrend <0.001).
Non-white ethnicity was associated with earlier menarche (multivariate beta = -7.80 months, 95% CI -9.90 to -5.70, Ptrend <0.001).
Higher childhood weight at age 7 was associated with earlier menarche (multivariate beta = -4.54 months per category, 95% CI -4.75 to -4.33).
Higher childhood height at age 7 was associated with earlier menarche (multivariate beta = -2.98 months per category, 95% CI -3.16 to -2.80).
More childhood exercise was associated with later menarche (multivariate beta = 1.18 months per 10 h/week, 95% CI 0.78–1.59).
Greater number of siblings was associated with later menarche (multivariate beta = 1.45 months per sibling, 95% CI 1.28–1.61).
Higher birth order was associated with earlier menarche after adjustment for sibship size (multivariate beta = -1.26 months, 95% CI -1.48 to -1.03).
Younger maternal age at birth was associated with earlier menarche (multivariate beta = 0.36 months per 5-year increase, 95% CI 0.19–0.53).
Twinning and prenatal pre-eclampsia/eclampsia exposure were significant in univariate analyses but not in the multivariate model.
No association with maternal age at birth in univariate analysis (Ptrend = 0.15) or vegetarian status before age 8 (P = 0.18).
A non-white girl who was much heavier and taller than peers at age 7 could reach menarche ~2 years earlier (difference = -22.8 months, 95% CI -25.0 to -20.7 months).
study_design: Cohort study (retrospective data collection via baseline questionnaire)
exposure_domain: Prenatal and childhood growth, lifestyle, and family factors (birthweight, maternal smoking, pre-eclampsia, breastfeeding, childhood weight/height, exercise, sibship size, birth order, ethnicity, maternal age)
limitations: Volunteer recruits rather than a population-based random sample, potentially biasing associations (particularly for ethnicity).
Retrospective self-reported data with possible recall bias, greater in older women.
Large amounts of missing data for breastfeeding and maternal smoking (available only when mother was also a study member).
